title: Queues vs streams, delivery guarantees and idempotent consumers
seriesDescription: Kafka and RabbitMQ semantics, delivery guarantees, outbox, CDC, dead letters and sagas. JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code and multi-correct questions.
description: RabbitMQ vs Kafka, partitions, consumer groups and offsets, durability settings, at-most/at-least/exactly-once and how to make consumers idempotent.
source: Apache Kafka documentation (consumer, producer and topic configs, log compaction); RabbitMQ docs (acknowledgements, dead letter exchanges); Designing Data-Intensive Applications

questions.prompt: A new analytics service must be able to read the last 7 days of order events from the beginning, and later services will need the same. Which broker model fits?

options.text: RabbitMQ classic queue: messages are removed from the queue once a consumer acks them.
options.why: Acked messages are gone, so a later service cannot replay history.

options.text: A transient in-memory topic with no persistence and no replay.
options.why: Nothing is retained, so there is nothing to read from the beginning.

options.text: A cron job polling the producer service for recent orders.
options.why: Polling the producer couples services and loses events the producer no longer keeps.

options.text: Kafka: a retained log, each group tracks its own offset.
options.why: Correct: records stay after being read, so any group can replay from an earlier offset.

questions.explanation: RabbitMQ is smart-broker routing and task distribution (exchanges, queues, per-message ack). Kafka is a dumb-broker, smart-consumer log with partitions, retention and offsets. RabbitMQ Streams exist too, but the classic queue consumes destructively.

questions.prompt: Match each Kafka concept with its meaning.

right.text: An ordered, append-only slice of a topic
Consumers that share the partitions of a topic, each partition owned by one member
The position of a record within a partition
Replicas that are caught up with the leader
The key that decides the topic name

questions.explanation: Ordering is only guaranteed inside a partition. A partition is consumed by at most one consumer of a given group at a time.

questions.prompt: A topic has 6 partitions. A consumer group has 9 consumers subscribed. How many consumers are actively receiving records?
questions.explanation: One partition goes to at most one consumer per group, so 6 are active and 3 sit idle. To add parallelism beyond 6 you need more partitions.

questions.prompt: For one partition the log end offset is 1500 and the group's committed offset is 1230 (the next record to read). What is the consumer lag in records?
questions.explanation: Lag = log end offset - committed offset = 1500 - 1230 = 270. Growing lag means consumers cannot keep up.

questions.prompt: A topic has replication factor 3 and min.insync.replicas = 2, and producers use acks=all. At most how many brokers holding the partition can be down while writes are still accepted?
questions.explanation: acks=all needs the in-sync replica count to be at least 2, so with 3 replicas only 1 can be lost. Losing 2 makes the producer get a NotEnoughReplicas error, trading availability for durability.

questions.prompt: Write the kafka-topics.sh command that creates the topic orders on localhost:9092 with 6 partitions, replication factor 3 and the topic config min.insync.replicas=2.
questions.explanation: Pair this topic config with producer acks=all. Other valid answers reorder the flags or use the .sh-less kafka-topics binary name. Replication factor 3 with min.insync.replicas 2 tolerates one broker failure without losing acknowledged writes.

questions.prompt: Complete the delivery semantics.
questions.text: Committing the offset {1} processing gives at-most-once and can lose messages; committing {2} processing gives at-least-once and can duplicate; Kafka transactions need consumers with isolation.level={3} to see only committed data.
questions.explanation: Exactly-once in Kafka means idempotent producer plus transactions within Kafka (consume-transform-produce). Side effects outside Kafka still need idempotent handling.

questions.prompt: Match each delivery semantic with what happens when the consumer crashes mid-flight.

right.text: The message may be lost because it was acknowledged before processing finished
The message is redelivered, so it may be processed twice
Redelivery happens but a dedup check makes the repeat harmless
The broker blocks all other consumers until the crash is fixed

questions.explanation: Effectively-once = at-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing. This is the pragmatic answer in interviews.

questions.prompt: Which statements about Kafka ordering and partitioning are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Order is guaranteed only within a single partition.
options.why: Correct: there is no ordering guarantee across partitions.

options.text: Records with the same key go to the same partition while the partition count stays the same.
options.why: Correct: the default partitioner hashes the key to a partition.

options.text: Adding partitions to a keyed topic can change which partition an existing key maps to.
options.why: Correct: the hash is taken modulo the partition count, so the mapping moves.

options.text: Adding more consumers than partitions increases group throughput.
options.why: Extra consumers beyond the partition count sit idle.

options.text: A topic guarantees total ordering of all records.
options.why: Only per-partition order is guaranteed.

questions.explanation: Choose the key by the entity whose order matters (for example orderId) and over-provision partitions early.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: A worker that acknowledges a queued task before running it can lose the task if the worker crashes mid-run.
questions.reason: Once a message is acknowledged the broker deletes it, so nothing is left to redeliver when the worker dies.

whys.a: Correct: The ack removes the only copy, so a crash after the ack but before completion loses the work.
whys.b: Not this one: Both are true but R is not the reason A holds does not describe this pair; R is actually the reason or is false.
whys.c: Not this one: A is true while R is false does not describe this pair; check the truth of R again.
whys.d: Not this one: A is false while R is true does not describe this pair; check the truth of A again.

questions.explanation: Acknowledging after completion gives at-least-once, so the task must then be idempotent. A worker killed by the operating system (for example out of memory) needs the broker to notice the lost connection before it redelivers.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: In RabbitMQ a message that has been acknowledged with basic.ack is redelivered if the consumer then crashes.
questions.reason: An ack tells the broker the message may be removed from the queue.

whys.a: Not this one: Both A and R are true and R explains A does not describe this pair; R does not explain A.
whys.b: Not this one: Both are true but R is not the reason A holds does not describe this pair; R is actually the reason or is false.
whys.c: Not this one: A is true while R is false does not describe this pair; check the truth of R again.
whys.d: Correct: A is false: after the ack the broker no longer holds the message. R is true and is exactly why it is not redelivered.

questions.explanation: Unacked messages are requeued when the channel closes. Ack after processing, not on receipt, unless you accept loss.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: A consumer group cannot have more active consumers than the topic has partitions.
questions.reason: Kafka retains records after they have been read.

whys.a: Not this one: Both A and R are true and R explains A does not describe this pair; R does not explain A.
whys.b: Correct: Both are true, but retention does not cause the limit: the one-owner-per-partition rule does.
whys.c: Not this one: A is true while R is false does not describe this pair; check the truth of R again.
whys.d: Not this one: A is false while R is true does not describe this pair; check the truth of A again.

questions.explanation: The one-owner-per-partition rule preserves ordering within a partition. Retention is what makes replay and extra groups possible.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: With an idempotent producer (the default since Kafka 3.0), records with the same key are always read in the order they were sent, provided the partition count does not change.
questions.reason: Kafka guarantees a global order across all partitions of a topic.

whys.a: Not this one: Both A and R are true and R explains A does not describe this pair; R does not explain A.
whys.b: Not this one: Both are true but R is not the reason A holds does not describe this pair; R is actually the reason or is false.
whys.c: Correct: A is true because the key pins the records to one partition, but R is false: there is no cross-partition order.
whys.d: Not this one: A is false while R is true does not describe this pair; check the truth of A again.

questions.explanation: Without idempotence, retries with several in-flight requests could reorder records; idempotent producers keep order with up to 5 in-flight requests per connection.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: A Kafka topic with cleanup.policy=compact keeps at least the latest record for every key.
questions.reason: Compaction deletes every record older than the retention period regardless of its key.

whys.a: Not this one: Both A and R are true and R explains A does not describe this pair; R does not explain A.
whys.b: Not this one: Both are true but R is not the reason A holds does not describe this pair; R is actually the reason or is false.
whys.c: Correct: A is true. R describes cleanup.policy=delete, not compaction.
whys.d: Not this one: A is false while R is true does not describe this pair; check the truth of A again.

questions.explanation: Compaction suits changelog or state topics (latest value per entity). Age-based removal is cleanup.policy=delete; both can be combined as compact,delete.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: With replication factor 3, min.insync.replicas=2 and acks=all, an acknowledged write survives the loss of one broker.
questions.reason: The partition leader only acknowledges once at least 2 in-sync replicas have the record.

whys.a: Correct: The acknowledgement implies two copies exist, so one broker can be lost without losing the record.
whys.b: Not this one: Both are true but R is not the reason A holds does not describe this pair; R is actually the reason or is false.
whys.c: Not this one: A is true while R is false does not describe this pair; check the truth of R again.
whys.d: Not this one: A is false while R is true does not describe this pair; check the truth of A again.

questions.explanation: Unclean leader election (unclean.leader.election.enable=true) would break the guarantee, which is why it stays off for durable topics.

questions.prompt: Table processed_messages(message_id text primary key). Write a PostgreSQL statement that records message id 'evt-42' and does nothing if it was already recorded.
questions.model: INSERT INTO processed_messages (message_id) VALUES ('evt-42') ON CONFLICT (message_id) DO NOTHING;
questions.explanation: Run it in the same transaction as the business side effect and check the affected row count: 0 rows means a duplicate, so skip the work. Other valid shapes: catch the unique violation, or use INSERT ... WHERE NOT EXISTS.

questions.prompt: Which is the most reliable deduplication key for an idempotent consumer?

options.text: A new UUID generated by the consumer each time a delivery arrives.
options.why: A fresh id per delivery makes every redelivery look new.

options.text: A producer-assigned event id stored with the effect.
options.why: Correct: the same event keeps the same id across redeliveries and retries.

options.text: The consumer's receive timestamp in milliseconds since epoch.
options.why: Each redelivery arrives at a different time, so it never matches.

options.text: A hash of the full message including the retry-attempt header.
options.why: The retry header changes between attempts, so the hash differs.

questions.explanation: Exactly-once delivery over an unreliable network is not achievable; an ack can be lost after the work is done. Dedup with a unique constraint on the event id in the same transaction as the effect.

questions.prompt: With default settings, a Kafka consumer takes 6 minutes to process each batch returned by poll(). The group keeps rebalancing and its offsets are never committed. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Processing exceeds max.poll.interval.ms (default 5 minutes), so the consumer is evicted from the group.
options.why: Correct: no poll within the interval makes the coordinator remove the member.

options.text: heartbeat.interval.ms of 3 seconds is too short, so heartbeats overload the coordinator.
options.why: Three-second heartbeats are the normal default and cheap.

options.text: session.timeout.ms of 45 seconds expires because processing blocks the heartbeat thread.
options.why: Heartbeats run on a background thread, so slow processing does not stop them.

options.text: The topic has more partitions than the group has consumers.
options.why: That just gives some consumers several partitions; it does not cause rebalances.

questions.explanation: Fixes: lower max.poll.records, raise max.poll.interval.ms, or hand slow work to another thread (and pause the partitions). Defaults per the Kafka docs: max.poll.interval.ms 300000, session.timeout.ms 45000 (3.0+), heartbeat.interval.ms 3000.

questions.prompt: A brand-new consumer group subscribes to an existing topic with no committed offsets and auto.offset.reset left at its default. Where does it start reading?

options.text: At the end of each partition, seeing only records produced after it joins.
options.why: Correct: the default is latest.

options.text: At the first retained record of each partition, replaying all stored history.
options.why: That is auto.offset.reset=earliest, not the default.

options.text: Nowhere: it raises an error and refuses to start.
options.why: An error only happens with auto.offset.reset=none.

options.text: At offset 0 of each partition, even if older segments were already deleted.
options.why: Offset 0 may no longer exist; earliest means the first retained offset.

questions.explanation: Classic trap: a new group with the default misses everything produced before it started. Use earliest for replay or backfill groups, and remember the setting applies only when no valid committed offset exists.

questions.prompt: In RabbitMQ a queue has a dead-letter exchange configured. Which events cause a message to be dead-lettered? Select all that apply.

options.text: A consumer rejects it with basic.nack or basic.reject and requeue=false.
options.why: Correct: a rejected message that is not requeued is dead-lettered.

options.text: Its per-message or per-queue TTL expires while it waits in the queue.
options.why: Correct: expiry dead-letters the message.

options.text: The queue has a maximum length and the message is dropped from the head to make room.
options.why: Correct: overflow from the head dead-letters the oldest message (default overflow behaviour).

options.text: A consumer acknowledges it with basic.ack after processing.
options.why: An ack simply removes the message; nothing is dead-lettered.

options.text: The publisher receives a confirm for it.
options.why: A publisher confirm is just broker acknowledgement of receipt.

questions.explanation: Quorum queues add a fourth cause: exceeding the delivery limit. The x-death header records the reason, queue and count, which is what a retry-with-delay topology reads.

questions.prompt: You need 100 MB/s of throughput. One partition sustains about 10 MB/s for producers and 20 MB/s for a consumer. What is the minimum number of partitions that satisfies both?
questions.explanation: Producers need 100/10 = 10 partitions and consumers need 100/20 = 5. Take the larger: 10. Add headroom for growth because partitions can be added later but remapping keyed ordering is painful.
